lead.headline: Why Two Messengers Flew From Moscow to Dublin in One Day
lead.deck: The talks about Ukraine’s war go on, and Europe wants a chair at the table.
body: When two people are too upset to talk, a friend sometimes carries messages between them. Countries do this too. On Thursday two Americans, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, carried messages about the war in Ukraine. They met Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin, in Moscow. Then they flew to Dublin, in Ireland, to report to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
The talking is not finished. A Russian official called the Moscow meeting useful and said the three-way talks will continue. Witkoff said, “I think progress was made.”

The hardest question has not moved. Putin said he would not soften his demands for land in Ukraine. Meanwhile, leaders were meeting in Dublin. About 40 countries there said choices about Europe’s safety should be made with Europe’s governments. Witkoff said Europeans will take part in the next stage.

world.headline: Indonesia’s Vice President Steps Down Over His School Papers
world.deck: Courts said his documents did not meet the rules for the job.
body: To run for Indonesia’s top jobs, a person must have finished high school, or schooling that counts the same. That rule is at the centre of a big change in Indonesia, a country in Southeast Asia.

On Thursday the vice president, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, resigned, which means he gave up his job. He is 39, the eldest son of former president Joko Widodo, and had served two years of a five-year term. He finished school in another country. Last month two top courts ruled that the papers he gave about that schooling did not meet the election rules.

On Wednesday, 120 lawmakers began steps that could have removed him. President Prabowo Subianto said he accepted the resignation with a “heavy heart.” There will be no new election. Instead, the president names two candidates. Then a large assembly of lawmakers elects one of them within 60 days.

us.headline: A Senate Race So Close It Took Days to Count
us.deck: Democrat Scott Colom won Mississippi with 49.2% of the vote.
body: Most elections are decided on the night of the vote. In the state of Mississippi, the race for a seat in the United States Senate was far too close for that. At the end of election night, just 65 votes separated the two candidates.
So officials spent days counting the ballots that were left. On Wednesday the result was clear. Scott Colom, a Democrat, had 49.2% of the vote. Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, had 48.7%.

Hyde-Smith phoned Colom to concede, which means to accept that she had lost. She said she respects “the decision of Mississippi voters.” Colom, 43, is a prosecutor, a lawyer who brings cases to court. He will be Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction, the years after the American Civil War. He promised to represent all Mississippians, including those who did not vote for him.
us.why: A tiny gap decided who speaks for a whole state.
also: Senate: Democrats will hold at least 55 seats from January; only Alaska’s race is still undecided.

india.headline: Onions Cost Twice as Much, and India’s Prices Cross a Limit
india.deck: Inflation reached 6.09% in October, above the central bank’s top limit of 6%.
body: Onions go into so many meals that their price is felt in kitchens across India. This October, onions cost more than twice as much as a year earlier. Garlic, ginger and lemons were much dearer too, though potatoes and cauliflower got cheaper.

Numbers like these come from a government check of prices in more than 1,400 city markets and more than 1,400 villages. On Thursday it reported October’s inflation, the yearly rise in prices: 6.09%, up from 5.54% the month before. For food alone it was 8.94%.

The Reserve Bank of India, the country’s central bank, tries to hold inflation between 2% and 6%. October broke through the top of that range, which had not happened for two years. To slow prices, the bank can raise its main interest rate, now 5.5%, which makes borrowing cost more. Its committee meets from 2 to 4 December. Economist Aditi Nayar said a rise is “almost certain.” She also warned that weak monsoon rains could keep food prices high.
india.why: Villages felt it most: prices there rose 6.63%, against 5.41% in cities.

lines.text: Good morning, and welcome to The Breakfast Table for Friday, November 13. Today: two messengers and two presidents, a vice president who gave up his job, and a vote count that came down to almost nothing.
Let’s start with the messengers. Who are they, and why were they flying around?

They are two Americans, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. When two people are too upset to talk, a friend sometimes carries messages between them. Countries do this too. These two carried messages about the war in Ukraine.
Where did they go?
First to Moscow, to meet Russia’s president, Vladimir Putin. Then to Dublin, in Ireland, to report to Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.
And did anything change?

The talking goes on. A Russian official called the Moscow meeting useful, and Witkoff said, I think progress was made. But the hardest question has not moved. Putin said he would not soften his demands for land in Ukraine.
Why were Europe’s leaders in the story?
They were meeting in Dublin. About 40 countries there said choices about Europe’s safety should be made with Europe’s governments. Witkoff said Europeans will take part in the next stage.
Now to Indonesia. The vice president has resigned. What happened?

To run for Indonesia’s top jobs, a person must have finished high school, or schooling that counts the same. The vice president, Gibran Rakabuming Raka, finished school in another country. Last month two top courts ruled that his papers about that schooling did not meet the election rules.
So he stepped down?
Yes, on Thursday. He is 39 and had served two years of a five-year term. A day earlier, 120 lawmakers had begun steps that could have removed him.
Does Indonesia vote again now?
No. There will be no new election. The president names two candidates. Then a large assembly of lawmakers elects one of them within 60 days.
Last story. An election in America took days to count?
It did. It was the race for a Senate seat in the state of Mississippi. At the end of election night, just 65 votes separated the two candidates.
That is hardly anything. What did officials do?
They spent days counting the ballots that were left. On Wednesday the result was clear. Scott Colom, a Democrat, had 49.2 percent. Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, a Republican, had 48.7 percent.
How did she take it?

She phoned Colom to concede, which means to accept that she had lost. She said she respects the decision of Mississippi voters. And Colom promised to represent all Mississippians, including those who did not vote for him.

When two people will not talk to each other, how can a go-between help, and what can go wrong?
That is The Breakfast Table for today. Thank you for listening, and enjoy your day.
